name: Inventory Observation and Valuation
title: Inventory Observation and Valuation
answer: Inventory observation and valuation covers the work of confirming that reported stock exists, is owned or controlled, and is carried at an amount the accounts can support. In continuous audit it extends beyond the traditional year end count to rolling checks on quantity, condition, location and cost through the period. sections.body: Inventory observation and valuation covers the work of confirming that reported stock exists, is owned or controlled, and is carried at an amount the accounts can support. In continuous audit it extends beyond the traditional year end count to rolling checks on quantity, condition, location and cost through the period. The topic sits inside The AI Accountant alongside the wider assurance material on this site, which currently runs to 229 compliance and regulation pages.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on the client's inventory subledger and warehouse systems, on count records and adjustment logs, and on the audit platform that holds sampling plans, workpapers and review notes. Where counting is automated, feeds come from barcode and RFID scanners, weigh scales, drone or fixed camera capture, and in some settings from robotic count units. Costing draws on purchase orders, standard cost tables, freight and duty records, and the valuation model held in the ERP.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Practitioners set materiality and risk by location and by stock class, then choose between physical count, cycle count evidence, analytical review of margins and turnover, and test counts at selected sites. Sampling is stratified by value and velocity, and results are reconciled to the perpetual records with any variance investigated before it is accepted. Valuation testing checks cost build up, overhead absorption, net realisable value against recent sales and ageing, and the treatment of slow moving or obsolete lines. Increasingly the count itself is supported by image recognition or scan data, with the auditor testing the accuracy of that capture rather than re-performing every count by hand.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk turn on who owns the goods, where title passes, and what the client can lawfully show an auditor, which matters for consignment stock, goods held on behalf of third parties, and stock in transit or in bonded warehouses. Provenance of count evidence has to be traceable to a device, a time, a location and a person, and any automated capture needs a record of the model or rule that produced the figure. Access to inventory systems, retention of count images and personal data captured in warehouses all fall under the same control and privacy expectations as the rest of the audit file.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward continuous observation rather than an annual event, with perpetual records, sensor data and periodic sampling replacing a single count date for many clients. That shift puts more weight on the reliability of the client's own systems and on the auditor's testing of those systems, and it raises questions about how much assurance a model driven count can carry. Expect closer linkage between inventory evidence and demand forecasting, write down triggers and going concern assessment as the data becomes available in near real time.
